result:
Solution 1 is wrong. It identifies $q^*$ with the upper critical exponent $\frac{N+\alpha}{N-2}$, which is the endpoint of the stated interval and does not produce a threshold in $\varepsilon$.

Solutions 2 and 3 both give $q^* = \frac{N+\alpha+2}{N}$, which is the $L^2$-critical (mass-critical) exponent for the Choquard term. Under the mass-preserving scaling $u_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{N/2}u(\lambda x)$, the Choquard energy $\iint \frac{|u(x)|^p|u(y)|^p}{|x-y|^{N-\alpha}}$ scales as $\lambda^{Np-N-\alpha}$. Balancing this against the kinetic scaling $\lambda^2$ gives $Np - N - \alpha = 2$, so $p = \frac{N+\alpha+2}{N}$. Since $g(s)\sim s^{q-1}$ near $0$, the effective Choquard power of the perturbation is $q$.

This matches the described behavior. Small $\varepsilon$ corresponds to large mass, so at or above the mass-critical exponent, ground states can fail to exist for small $\varepsilon$ and appear only for $\varepsilon > \varepsilon_q$. Below it, existence holds for all $\varepsilon$.

I did not fully verify this against the source paper. A mixed-term scaling heuristic (pairing $|u|^{p_l}$ with $|u|^q$) gives $\frac{N+\alpha+4}{N}$ instead, but I consider the standard mass-critical identification more reliable here. Solution 3 is the better-justified of the two correct-valued solutions, though Solution 2 reaches the same value.

CHOICE: 3
